items.stem: Which is the definition of magnetic flux through an area A perpendicular to a field B?
items.answer: Φ = BA
items.markingKey: Flux = flux density × area normal to the field.

items.stem: Explain why the flux through a coil depends on the angle between the coil and the field.
items.answer: Only the component of B perpendicular to the plane of the coil passes through it: Φ = BA cos θ (θ between B and the normal); the flux is maximum when the coil is perpendicular to the field and zero when parallel.
items.markingKey: only perpendicular component [1]; max when perpendicular, zero when parallel [1] [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between magnetic flux density and magnetic flux.
items.answer: Flux density B is the force per unit current per unit length (T), a measure of field strength at a point; flux Φ = BA is the total "amount of field" passing through an area (Wb).
items.markingKey: B: field strength at a point, T [1]; Φ = BA through an area, Wb [1] [2]

items.stem: A circular coil of diameter 8.0 cm has 150 turns and is placed with the normal to its plane at 45° to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.15 T. Calculate the flux linkage.
items.markingKey: NΦ = NBA cos θ = 150 × 0.15 × 5.03 × 10⁻³ × cos 45° = 0.0800 Wb. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A circular coil of diameter 3.0 cm has 500 turns and is placed with the normal to its plane at 60° to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.050 T. Calculate the area of the coil, the flux through one turn and the flux linkage.

A coil of 100 turns, each of area 4.0 × 10⁻³ m², is held with its plane perpendicular to a uniform field of 0.25 T. (a) Define magnetic flux. (b) Calculate the flux through one turn. (c) Calculate the flux linkage when the coil is rotated through 60°.
items.answer: (a) Product of flux density and area normal to the field (Φ = BA). (b) 1.00 × 10⁻³ Wb (c) 0.050 Wb
items.markingKey: (a) Product of flux density and area normal to the field (Φ = BA) [1] (b) Φ = BA: 1.00 × 10⁻³ Wb [1] (c) cos 60° = 0.5 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 0.050 Wb with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: What is the unit of magnetic flux?
items.answer: weber (Wb)
items.markingKey: 1 Wb = 1 T m².

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A coil of 200 turns and area 5.0 × 10⁻³ m² is perpendicular to a field of 0.40 T. What is the flux linkage? (b) A flat coil is rotated from perpendicular to parallel with a uniform magnetic field. The flux through it …
items.answer: (a) 0.40 Wb (b) falls from a maximum to zero
items.markingKey: (a) NΦ = NBA = 200 × 0.40 × 5.0 × 10⁻³. (b) Φ = BA cos θ, where θ is the angle between B and the normal.

items.stem: Explain why a coil with more turns gives a larger flux linkage in the same field.
items.answer: Each turn has the same flux Φ through it; flux linkage NΦ adds the contributions of all N turns.
items.markingKey: same flux per turn [1]; linkage = NΦ ∝ N [1] [2]

items.stem: A flat coil in a uniform magnetic field is turned so that the angle between the field and the normal to the coil changes from 90° to 0°. Explain how the magnetic flux through the coil changes, and give the ratio of the final flux to the initial flux if it exists.
items.answer: Φ = BA cos θ; flux changes from 0.000000000000000061BA to 1.0BA
items.markingKey: Φ = BA cos θ [1]; correct direction of change [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why the flux through a coil depends on the angle between the coil and the field. (b) Distinguish between magnetic flux density and magnetic flux.
items.answer: (a) Only the component of B perpendicular to the plane of the coil passes through it: Φ = BA cos θ (θ between B and the normal); the flux is maximum when the coil is perpendicular to the field and zero when parallel. (b) Flux density B is the force per unit current per unit length (T), a measure of field strength at a point; flux Φ = BA is the total "amount of field" passing through an area (Wb).
items.markingKey: (a) only perpendicular component [1]; max when perpendicular, zero when parallel [1] [2] (b) B: field strength at a point, T [1]; Φ = BA through an area, Wb [1] [2]

(c) Calculate the flux linkage. (d) Calculate the flux linkage when the coil is rotated through 60°. (e) Explain why the flux through the coil and the flux linkage have the same unit.
items.answer: (a) Product of flux density and area normal to the field (Φ = BA). (b) 4.00 × 10⁻⁴ Wb (c) 0.12 Wb (d) 0.060 Wb (e) N is a pure number (no unit), so NΦ has the unit of Φ (Wb).
items.markingKey: (a) Product of flux density and area normal to the field (Φ = BA) [1] (b) Φ = BA: 4.00 × 10⁻⁴ Wb [1] (c) NΦ: 0.12 Wb [1] (d) cos 60° = 0.5 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 0.060 Wb with unit [1] [2] (e) N is a pure number (no unit), so NΦ has the unit of Φ (Wb) [1]

items.stem: Faraday's law states that the induced e.m.f. is proportional to …
options: the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage
items.answer: the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage
items.markingKey: E = −d(NΦ)/dt.

items.stem: Explain, using Lenz's law, why work must be done to push a magnet into a coil connected in a closed circuit.
items.answer: The induced current makes the coil end a like pole that repels the magnet, opposing its motion; work must be done against this force, and this work becomes electrical energy (then thermal energy) in the circuit.
items.markingKey: induced pole repels / opposes motion [1]; work done converted to electrical energy [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why no e.m.f. is induced in a coil when a magnet is held stationary inside it.
items.answer: E is proportional to the rate of change of flux linkage; when the magnet is stationary the flux linkage is constant, so there is no e.m.f.
items.markingKey: flux linkage constant [1]; no rate of change so E = 0 [1] [2]

items.stem: A coil of 500 turns and area 2.5 × 10⁻³ m² is perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.40 T. The field is reduced uniformly to zero in 0.10 s. Calculate the magnitude of the average induced e.m.f.
items.markingKey: E = Δ(NΦ)/Δt = 500 × 2.5 × 10⁻³ × 0.40/0.10 = 5.0 V. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A coil of 50 turns and area 8.0 × 10⁻³ m² is perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.60 T. The field is reversed uniformly to 0.20 T in the opposite direction in 0.40 s. Calculate the change in flux linkage and the average induced e.m.f.

A coil of 100 turns and area 4.0 × 10⁻³ m² is perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.60 T. The field is reduced uniformly to zero in 0.20 s. The coil is connected to form a circuit of total resistance 20 Ω. (a) Calculate the average induced e.m.f. (b) Calculate the average current and the charge that flows. (c) Explain, using Lenz's law, the direction of the induced current.
items.answer: (a) 1.2 V (b) I = 0.060 A; Q = 0.012 C (c) the induced current produces a field that opposes the change, i.e. in the direction of the original field (it tries to maintain the decreasing flux)
items.markingKey: (a) E = Δ(NΦ)/Δt = 1.2 V [1] (b) I = E/R = 0.060 A [1]; Q = It = 0.012 C [1] (c) opposes change [1]; field direction of original field [1] [5]

items.stem: A coil of 200 turns and area 5.0 × 10⁻³ m² is pulled out of a uniform magnetic field of 0.30 T, perpendicular to its plane, in 0.25 s. (a) Calculate the initial flux linkage. (b) State Lenz's law and use it to explain why a force is needed to pull the coil out. (c) Suggest how the induced e.m.f. could be doubled.
items.answer: (a) 0.30 Wb (b) Induced current opposes the change: it produces a force opposing the motion, so work must be done. (c) Pull it out in half the time, double the turns, or double B or A.
items.markingKey: (a) NBA: 0.30 Wb [1] (b) Lenz statement [1]; opposing force on coil [1] [2] (c) Pull it out in half the time, double the turns, or double B or A [1]

items.stem: Lenz's law is a consequence of the conservation of …
items.answer: energy
items.markingKey: The induced current opposes the change; otherwise energy would be created.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) In E = −d(NΦ)/dt, the minus sign represents … (b) State Lenz's law.
items.answer: (a) Lenz's law: the induced e.m.f. opposes the change producing it (b) The direction of the induced e.m.f. (current) is such as to oppose the change producing it.
items.markingKey: (a) Direction of e.m.f. opposes the change. (b) opposes the change causing it [1]

items.stem: Explain how a metal rod moving through a magnetic field has an e.m.f. induced across it, in terms of forces on electrons.
items.answer: Free electrons in the rod move with it at velocity v; each experiences a force Bev along the rod, so electrons collect at one end, creating a p.d. (e.m.f.) until the electric force balances the magnetic force.
items.markingKey: force Bev on free electrons along rod [1]; charge separation gives e.m.f. [1] [2]

items.stem: Derive the expression E = BLv for a rod moving perpendicular to a field.
items.answer: In time Δt the rod sweeps area LvΔt, so the flux cut ΔΦ = BLvΔt; E = ΔΦ/Δt = BLv.
items.markingKey: area swept = LvΔt [1]; E = ΔΦ/Δt = BLv [1] [2]

items.stem: A magnet is dropped through a long vertical copper tube. Explain why it falls more slowly than when dropped outside the tube.
items.answer: The falling magnet causes changing flux in the tube walls, inducing eddy currents; by Lenz's law these produce a field that opposes the motion, giving an upward force on the magnet.
items.markingKey: changing flux induces currents [1]; currents oppose motion (Lenz) [1] [2]

items.stem: A bar magnet is moved past a pickup coil on a guitar test rig. The speed at which the magnet is moved is reduced to one third while the number of turns stays the same. Predict, with a reason, how the magnitude of the induced e.m.f. changes.
items.answer: The magnitude of the induced e.m.f. becomes one third.
items.markingKey: Using E = N ΔΦ/Δt: magnitude of the induced e.m.f. ∝ speed at which the magnet is moved; factor = 0.333 = 0.333. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: In a simple a.c. generator, the e.m.f. is a maximum when the plane of the coil is …
options: at any angle; it is constant
items.answer: parallel to the magnetic field
items.markingKey: Flux linkage is zero but its rate of change is greatest.

items.stem: Explain why the e.m.f. of a rotating coil generator is zero when the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field.
items.answer: At that instant the flux linkage is a maximum and momentarily not changing (the sides move parallel to the field), so the rate of change of flux linkage, and hence the e.m.f., is zero.
items.markingKey: flux linkage maximum [1]; rate of change zero [1] [2]

items.stem: A generator coil of 200 turns, each of area 1.0 × 10⁻² m², rotates at 5.0 revolutions per second in a uniform magnetic field of 0.10 T. Work out the peak e.m.f.
items.markingKey: E₀ = BANω = 0.10 × 1.0 × 10⁻² × 200 × 2π × 5.0 = 6.28 V. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A model generator has a coil of 200 turns, each of area 1.0 × 10⁻² m², rotating at 50 revolutions per second in a field of 0.10 T. (a) Calculate the maximum flux linkage. (b) State the position of the coil when the e.m.f. is a maximum and explain why.
items.answer: (a) 0.20 Wb (b) Plane of the coil parallel to the field: flux linkage is zero but changing fastest.
items.markingKey: (a) NBA: 0.20 Wb [1] (b) parallel to field [1]; max rate of change of flux linkage [1] [2]

items.stem: Why is the core of a transformer made of thin insulated sheets (laminations)?
options: to make the core lighter only
to increase the resistance of the coils
to reduce eddy currents in the core
items.answer: to reduce eddy currents in the core
items.markingKey: Laminations increase resistance to eddy current loops, reducing heating.

items.stem: Explain how eddy currents produce a braking force on a metal disc rotating between magnet poles.
items.answer: Parts of the disc move through the field, cutting flux, so e.m.f.s and circulating eddy currents are induced; by Lenz's law the forces on these currents oppose the motion, slowing the disc; kinetic energy becomes thermal energy.
items.markingKey: eddy currents induced by changing flux [1]; force opposes motion (Lenz), KE → thermal [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why cutting slots in a metal plate makes it swing more freely through a magnetic field.
items.answer: The slots break up the paths of eddy currents, increasing resistance and reducing the size of the currents; the opposing force and energy loss are smaller.
items.markingKey: slots interrupt eddy current paths [1]; smaller currents, less damping [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe how a microphone or guitar pickup uses electromagnetic induction.
items.answer: A vibrating diaphragm (or steel string) moves a coil relative to a magnet (or changes the flux through a coil); the changing flux linkage induces an e.m.f. that varies in time with the vibration.
items.markingKey: relative motion / changing flux [1]; induced e.m.f. follows vibration [1] [2]

items.stem: A generator coil of 500 turns, each of area 2.0 × 10⁻³ m², rotates at 50 revolutions per second in a uniform magnetic field of 0.20 T. Work out the peak e.m.f.

items.stem: A generator coil of 200 turns, each of area 2.0 × 10⁻² m², rotates at 25 revolutions per second in a uniform magnetic field of 0.050 T. Calculate the angular speed and the peak e.m.f., and state the frequency of the alternating e.m.f.

items.stem: A model generator has a coil of 200 turns, each of area 1.0 × 10⁻² m², rotating at 50 revolutions per second in a field of 0.15 T. items.answer: (a) Plane of the coil parallel to the field: flux linkage is zero but changing fastest. (b) Current flows in the coil; by Lenz's law the force on it opposes the rotation, so more work is needed (converted to electrical energy).

items.stem: The flux linkage of a coil falls uniformly from 0.60 Wb to zero in 0.20 s. What is the magnitude of the induced e.m.f.?

Answer both parts. (a) Derive the expression E = BLv for a rod moving perpendicular to a field. (b) A magnet is dropped through a long vertical copper tube. Explain why it falls more slowly than when dropped outside the tube.
items.answer: (a) In time Δt the rod sweeps area LvΔt, so the flux cut ΔΦ = BLvΔt; E = ΔΦ/Δt = BLv. (b) The falling magnet causes changing flux in the tube walls, inducing eddy currents; by Lenz's law these produce a field that opposes the motion, giving an upward force on the magnet.
items.markingKey: (a) area swept = LvΔt [1]; E = ΔΦ/Δt = BLv [1] [2] (b) changing flux induces currents [1]; currents oppose motion (Lenz) [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Derive the expression E = BLv for a rod moving perpendicular to a field. (b) Explain why no e.m.f. is induced in a coil when a magnet is held stationary inside it.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why the flux through a coil depends on the angle between the coil and the field. (b) Distinguish between magnetic flux density and magnetic flux.
items.answer: (a) Only the component of B perpendicular to the plane of the coil passes through it: Φ = BA cos θ (θ between B and the normal); the flux is maximum when the coil is perpendicular to the field and zero when parallel. items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain, using Lenz's law, why work must be done to push a magnet into a coil connected in a closed circuit. (b) A magnet is dropped through a long vertical copper tube. Explain why it falls more slowly than when dropped outside the tube.
items.answer: (a) The induced current makes the coil end a like pole that repels the magnet, opposing its motion; work must be done against this force, and this work becomes electrical energy (then thermal energy) in the circuit. (b) The falling magnet causes changing flux in the tube walls, inducing eddy currents; by Lenz's law these produce a field that opposes the motion, giving an upward force on the magnet.
items.markingKey: (a) induced pole repels / opposes motion [1]; work done converted to electrical energy [1] [2] (b) changing flux induces currents [1]; currents oppose motion (Lenz) [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain how a metal rod moving through a magnetic field has an e.m.f. induced across it, in terms of forces on electrons. (b) A magnet is dropped through a long vertical copper tube. Explain why it falls more slowly than when dropped outside the tube.
items.answer: (a) Free electrons in the rod move with it at velocity v; each experiences a force Bev along the rod, so electrons collect at one end, creating a p.d. (e.m.f.) until the electric force balances the magnetic force. (b) The falling magnet causes changing flux in the tube walls, inducing eddy currents; by Lenz's law these produce a field that opposes the motion, giving an upward force on the magnet.
items.markingKey: (a) force Bev on free electrons along rod [1]; charge separation gives e.m.f. [1] [2] (b) changing flux induces currents [1]; currents oppose motion (Lenz) [1] [2]
